claim.pdf_says: In the ACCEPT Format 3 AT phrase both alternatives of the inner brace are underlined: 'COLUMN' (underlined) over 'COL' (underlined).
claim.why_it_matters: COL is a required (reserved) word abbreviation of COLUMN -- 14.9.1 prints it underlined, and 14.9.11 (page 640) records it in its figure note as underlined. The markdown underlines COLUMN but not COL in the very same brace, so a reader/implementor derives that COL is a user-defined word rather than a reserved alternative. Loss of underlining changes the grammar.

verdict.reasoning: Independently confirmed at the glyph level, and the attempts to refute all failed. (1) PDF: rendered spec_p607.png at 300 dpi (printed page 577) and cropped the AT phrase to a 3x upscale. Inside the inner brace I see TWO separate horizontal rules, each exactly word-width and sitting at underline depth below its own baseline: one spanning C..N directly under COLUMN, and a second, visibly shorter one spanning C..L directly under COL. They are not one shared rule and not a fraction bar -- a fraction bar would be a single rule centered in the vertical gap and spanning the full brace content width; here COLUMN's rule hugs COLUMN's baseline at COLUMN's width and COL has its own independent rule below it. So the PDF underlines BOTH alternatives, exactly as claimed. (2) Markdown: the claim quotes specs/ISO_COBOL.md:25263 verbatim -- '\underline{\text{COLUMN}} \\ \text{COL}'. COLUMN carries \underline{}, COL does not. No misquote of either source. (3) Not a formatting/convention artifact: this transcription IS tracking underlining in this very figure -- it underlines LINE but deliberately leaves NUMBER plain, and leaves AT plain, both matching the PDF. So the missing \underline{} on COL is an affirmative false distinction drawn inside a single brace, not a wholesale convention drop. (4) Not recoverable from adjacent text: I read specs/ISO_COBOL.md:25248-25273; page 607 carries no figure note that restores COL's underlining, so \underline{} is the only signal present. (5) Meaning genuinely changes: per ISO 5.2.2 (line 2628) keywords 'are shown in uppercase and underlined in general formats [and] are required in order to select the functionality', while per ISO 5.2.3 (line 2641) optional words 'are shown in uppercase and not underlined [and] may be written to add clarity'. A non-underlined COL therefore reads as an omittable optional word rather than a required keyword, yielding the nonsensical grammar 'AT { COLUMN | <omittable> } NUMBER ...'. (6) Corroborated against siblings: the transcription's own figure notes for every other occurrence of this same brace record COL as underlined -- line 17096 (screen description entry Format 1: 'COL is the required minimum abbreviation of COLUMN'), line 17868 (COLUMN clause Format 2, re-rendered at 600 dpi), and line 26514 (14.9.11 DISPLAY, page 640: 'Underlined required words: DISPLAY, LINE, COLUMN, COL, ...'). Page 607 is the lone outlier. Fix: '\underline{\text{COL}}'.
verdict.corrected_description: Real, with one correction to the stated rationale. The lost underline on COL does NOT make it read as a user-defined word -- user-defined words are printed lowercase and hyphenated in general formats (identifier-4, integer-2). Under ISO 5.2.2 / 5.2.3 the actual misreading is required keyword vs OPTIONAL WORD: an uppercase word that is not underlined is by definition an optional word that may be omitted, so the markdown states that the second alternative of the COLUMN/COL brace can be written as nothing, and that COL is not required to select the functionality. COL is in fact the required minimum abbreviation of COLUMN (a keyword), as the transcription itself records at lines 17096, 17868 and 26514. Everything else in the claim -- the PDF underlines both, the markdown underlines only COLUMN, and the loss is normative -- is confirmed. Separately noted while verifying, and OUT OF SCOPE for this claim: the immediately following display block at specs/ISO_COBOL.md:25265 drops the underlines on EXCEPTION (both occurrences) and NOT, which the PDF prints underlined.
